clue.text: Ornamental coverings undone in striptease

indicators.note: undone, like a garment unfastened, says the letters of the next word are taken apart and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A stripper's routine leaves some decorative wall hangings in disarray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'undone' turns the ten letters of STRIPTEASE into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Woven pictorial hangings were used to decorate and cover the walls of grand rooms.

clue.text: Building we put in high-rise area

indicators.note: put in tells us the word we is placed inside the hilly area

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, an area of high ground rising above the moor
taken as written

explanation.surface: A planner describes adding a block to a district of tall buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high-rise' suggests a skyscraper, but here it means rising ground: TOR is a rocky hilltop, as on Dartmoor in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall structure such as a church steeple or castle keep is a kind of building.

clue.text: Father ordered again to part of South America

parts.note: pa is an informal word for a father

indicators.note: ordered means the letters of again and to are put into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A father is told once more to travel to a southern region of the continent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' looks like a command to Father; it is the anagram signal working on AGAIN plus TO to give TAGONIA.
explanation.definitionFit: The region at the southern tip of the continent is shared by Argentina and Chile.

clue.text: Expert solver concerned with 26 squires

parts.note: the great fictional detective appears in the Conan Doyle story The Reigate Squires, and 26 across is that Surrey town

explanation.surface: A clever puzzler is said to be connected with some country gentlemen from a numbered place.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to the answer at 26 across, the Surrey town; Conan Doyle's story about it is titled The Reigate Squires (also known as The Reigate Puzzle).
explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's consulting detective is the archetypal expert at solving mysteries, including the case set in that Surrey town.

clue.text: Is Bismarck following right course?

indicators.note: following places the words before it after the abbreviation for right

parts.note: taken as written
Otto von Bismarck was the nineteenth-century German chancellor

explanation.surface: A question about whether the German statesman Bismarck took the correct path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' reads as a route or policy, but it is a course of a meal. Bismarck's first name was Otto.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian rice dish cooked in stock is served as one course of a meal.

clue.text: Nasty part of scene? Yes, or environment

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone agrees that a particular setting or surrounding is unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts with the last E of 'scene', takes all of 'Yes' and 'or', and ends with the E of 'environment'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ugly that spoils a view is a nasty sight; the clue uses the adjective loosely for the unsightly thing itself.

clue.text: Term equivalent to a score of forty

definitions.meaning: at some British schools, such as Eton, a school term is called by this name

definitions.text: equivalent to a score of forty
definitions.meaning: a score is twenty, which is one of two equal parts of forty

explanation.definitionFit: Some public schools divide the year into periods with this name, and twenty is precisely a fraction, one of two equal parts, of forty.

clue.text: Make amends in early afternoon

definitions.meaning: to make reparation or put right a wrong
split into two words, it gives the time one o'clock in the afternoon

explanation.definitionFit: To expiate a wrong is to make reparation, and split in two the letters say the hour just past midday.

clue.text: No cover charge, we hear, in Australia

indicators.note: we hear says the letters are spelt as the spoken phrase sounds

parts.note: a mantle is a cloak or cover, and free means no charge, giving free mantle

explanation.surface: A traveller reports that there is no charge for entry or cover over in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover charge' looks like a restaurant fee; split it as 'cover' (MANTLE) and 'No charge' (FREE). The definition is just 'in Australia': a place found there, the port near Perth.
explanation.definitionFit: The port city at the mouth of the Swan River near Perth lies on Australia's west coast.

clue.text: Relatives making contact with us, being in the money

parts.note: kissing is a way of touching or making contact, as balls do in snooker

indicators.note: being in says the word us sits inside the money

parts.note: coins are money
taken as written

explanation.surface: Family members get in touch with us when they are rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being in the money' reads as being wealthy, but 'being in' is a container signal; 'making contact' is the kissing of snooker balls.
explanation.definitionFit: Kissing cousins are relations close enough to greet one another with a kiss.

clue.text: See it in every quarter, one repeated

indicators.note: in says the word it goes inside the compass points

parts.note: the four compass quarters W, N, E and S, with the last one repeated
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to look for it everywhere, with one place visited twice.
explanation.walkthrough: The four quarters are the compass points, taken here in the order west, north, east, south, with the last doubled because 'one repeated'.
explanation.definitionFit: To see an event, such as a crime or a signature, is to be present as an observer of it.

clue.text: Summary — record one from my point of view

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
I is the Roman numeral for one
to me means in my opinion

explanation.surface: Someone offers a brief record of their own perspective.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from my point of view' looks like a link phrase, but it supplies TO ME.
explanation.definitionFit: An abridgement or abstract of a longer work is an older sense of the word; it also means a perfect example.

clue.text: Right one with energy allowed to work for operatic company

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
go means energy or vigour
let means allowed
taken as written

explanation.surface: A correct and lively singer is permitted to join an opera company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work' looks like a verb to do with a job; it is a noun, an opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's opera about the hunchbacked court jester is a staple of opera houses.

clue.text: Italian city in parts stuck into sea

indicators.note: stuck into says the letters of the small word are inserted into the large one
parts says the small word is split, its two letters going in at separate places

parts.note: taken as written
the first part of the word in
the second part of the word in

explanation.surface: Pieces of a Tuscan town have been put into the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in parts' says the word IN is split: its I goes after the S of SEA and its N after the E.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tuscan city is famous for its Palio horse race and medieval cathedral.

clue.text: Burns' mouse was in this sort of grass

definitions.meaning: in Robert Burns's poem To a Mouse, the wee beastie has a terrified state in its breast
a genus of grasses, including millet, shares the name

explanation.definitionFit: Burns's mouse is in a state of terror, and millet belongs to a grass genus of this name.

clue.text: Ruler's head is empty of wine

indicators.note: is here means holds or contains, so the head wraps round the other pieces

parts.note: pate is an old word for the head
O is a circle with nothing inside, so it stands for empty or nothing
tent is a deep-red Spanish wine

explanation.surface: A monarch's head has no drink left in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' works as a container signal, the head holding the rest. Tent is an old name for a deep-red wine from Spain, now known mainly from crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch or sovereign holding absolute power is a potentate.

clue.text: Observe Virgo then, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters of Virgo then might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: An astronomer is told to look at the constellation Virgo next.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges VIRGO and THEN. The definition is loose: the surface suggests stargazing, and the answer is the time over which the night-watcher would observe.
explanation.definitionFit: Watching the stars means keeping up a vigil through the dark hours until morning, which is what the word describes.

clue.text: Settle down at end of painting artist takes six to gallery

indicators.note: at end of picks out the final letter of painting

parts.note: RA stands for Royal Academician, an artist
VI is the Roman numeral for six
the Tate is the London art gallery

explanation.surface: After finishing a painting, an artist brings six works to an exhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: Painting, artist and gallery paint an art-world scene; the pieces are G, RA (Royal Academician), VI and TATE, the London gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: To sink or be drawn downwards, as sediment does, is to settle under gravity.

clue.text: Willing to learn each entry in set of figures

indicators.note: entry in means the word each goes inside the set of figures

parts.note: a table is a set of figures arranged in rows and columns

explanation.surface: Someone keen to study counts every item in a list of numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entry' looks like an item in a table, but it signals putting EACH into TABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil who can be instructed and is ready to absorb a lesson is receptive.

clue.text: What's finest about west shown in broadcast?

parts.note: the finest thing is the best
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A question about which westerns are the best ones on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' suggests television; here it means scattered, as seed is.
explanation.definitionFit: To scatter something over a surface, as seed thrown by hand is sown, is an old sense.

clue.text: Such parts as this are damaged with loud instrument

indicators.note: damaged says the letters of are are knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a drum is a loud percussion instrument

explanation.surface: Someone warns that these delicate body parts suffer harm from noisy instruments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' rearranges ARE to give EAR. The surface truthfully says loud music can harm this part of the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: The thin membrane inside the ear is a body part that loud noise can harm.

clue.text: College girl in Ireland

definitions.meaning: a county in the west of Ireland

explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs to a Cambridge college, is a female first name, and is a county on Ireland's west coast.

clue.text: He is, for example, madly in love

indicators.note: in says the rearranged letters go inside the word for love

parts.note: love means nil, a score of zero in tennis

indicators.note: madly says the abbreviation for example is jumbled

explanation.surface: A man, for example, is crazily in love.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is a zero score in tennis. The surface makes 'He' a lovesick man; it is the definition of a man's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name, so a male person may be referred to as he.

clue.text: Maiden? Rarely seen when he was in

definitions.text: Maiden? Rarely seen when he was in

parts.words: Maiden? Rarely seen when he was in
parts.note: in cricket a maiden is an over with no runs scored, and the great Victorian batsman scored so freely that few were bowled while he was batting

explanation.surface: A young woman was hardly ever seen while a certain man was at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maiden' suggests a young woman; in cricket a maiden is an over from which no runs are scored. W.G. Grace was the most famous English cricketer of the Victorian era.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Victorian cricketer piled up runs so freely that bowlers rarely managed scoreless overs against him.

clue.text: Beginning to grow out in appropriate season

indicators.note: in says the word out is placed inside the season

parts.note: spring is the season when plants start to shoot, so it is appropriate here
taken as written

explanation.surface: Shoots start appearing at the right time of year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out in' reads as a phrase, but 'in' is the container signal; 'appropriate' tells us which season is meant, the one when shoots appear.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants putting out new shoots are starting to grow.

clue.text: Divine visitors have no end of enjoyment

indicators.note: have no says the letter that follows is removed from the visitors

parts.note: guests are visitors

indicators.note: end of picks the final letter of enjoyment

explanation.surface: Holy visitors fail to enjoy themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divine' looks like an adjective meaning holy; it is the verb, to work out by intuition. GUESTS loses a T, the last letter of 'enjoyment'.
explanation.definitionFit: To divine something is to discover it by intuition or conjecture.

clue.text: But he may find his effort rewarding

definitions.text: But he may find his effort rewarding

parts.words: But he may find his effort rewarding
parts.note: a non-professional is not paid, but may still find personal satisfaction in what he does

explanation.surface: An unpaid enthusiast takes satisfaction from his work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewarding' plays on two senses: financially rewarding, which this person's effort is not, and satisfying, which it may be.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who takes part for love rather than pay gets satisfaction, not money, from his efforts.

clue.text: Crooked-sounding entrance to garden town in Surrey

indicators.note: sounding says the letters follow the sound of the words, not their spelling

parts.note: wry means crooked or twisted
a gate is an entrance to a garden

explanation.surface: A town in Surrey has a bent gateway at the entrance to its garden.
explanation.walkthrough: '-sounding' attached to 'Crooked' says WRY is spelt as it sounds, matching the first syllable of the town, pronounced 'rye-gate'. Surrey is a county just south of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The market town lies at the foot of the North Downs in the county south of London.

clue.text: Like the following, but not the preceding, number

definitions.text: Like the following, but not the preceding, number

parts.words: Like the following, but not the preceding, number
parts.note: the enumeration that follows the clue, 4, is divisible by two, while the clue's own number before it, 27, is not

explanation.surface: Someone compares two figures, saying one resembles the next but not the last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the following' number is the (4) printed after the clue; 'the preceding' number is the clue number 27 in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Four can be divided by two with nothing left over, while twenty-seven cannot.

clue.text: Vessels with no man-servant?

parts.note: the saying no man can serve two employers at once is read as a description of ships with a pair of upright spars

explanation.surface: Some ships sail without a valet on board.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'no man can serve two masters' (Matthew 6:24) is hinted at by 'no man-servant'; masts on a sailing ship give the vessel sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailing ships rigged with a pair of masts are described as two-masted, and the biblical proverb names the pair of employers.
